name: Aspirin mask

lead: The aspirin mask is a home paste made from crushed aspirin tablets, applied to the face by people who want clearer, less red skin and fewer breakouts.

The reasoning runs through salicylic acid, a common acne ingredient: aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid and is broken down to salicylic acid in the body. Users expect a similar pore-clearing, calming effect on the skin. Salicylic acid itself is studied for acne; no studies of the aspirin mask were found.

paras: People mix crushed tablets with water or another base into a paste, leave it on for a short time as a wash-off mask, and rinse. It is used as an occasional spot or whole-face treatment alongside a normal cleanser and moisturizer. Users usually look for a change in redness within hours and in breakouts over repeated uses.

The documented warnings about aspirin concern oral use, such as stomach irritation and bleeding risk and avoidance by people with aspirin allergy. Effects of a topical aspirin paste are not described in the sources reviewed, so irritation on the face is possible but not characterised. People allergic to aspirin or salicylates have reason to avoid it.

angle.text: Users crush aspirin into a paste and apply it to the face for clearer, less red skin, reasoning from aspirin's relation to salicylic acid. Salicylic acid itself is studied for acne; the aspirin mask has not been.

lead: An aspirin mask is a home paste made by crushing uncoated aspirin tablets, mixing them with water or another base such as honey or yogurt, and leaving the paste on the face briefly. People use it on acne spots and red, oily skin, hoping to calm breakouts and leave a clearer complexion. The reasoning is that aspirin is chemically related to salicylic acid, a standard acne ingredient.

Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, made by acetylating salicylic acid, and the body readily converts it back to salicylic acid. Salicylic acid itself is a keratolytic and comedolytic: it loosens the outer skin layer and makes cells shed more readily, which helps keep pores from clogging, and cosmetic products use it for acne [1]. Proponents' chain runs from crushed aspirin to salicylate on the skin, to less clogged pores and less inflammation, to fewer visible blemishes.
No studies of aspirin masks were found. Wikipedia's aspirin article mentions topical aspirin only in connection with possible effectiveness for some neuropathic pain.
infobox: Salicylic acid, a standard OTC acne ingredient [1]

paras: Aspirin is produced by acetylating salicylic acid and is readily converted to it in the body. Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent used in cosmetics for acne, seborrhoeic dermatitis, calluses and keratosis pilaris, and it also modulates COX-1 and reduces pro-inflammatory prostaglandin formation [1]. Salicylic acid is a metabolite of aspirin and long served as the starting material for making it; the compound traces back to willow bark, with salicin isolated by Johann Buchner in 1828 [1]. Commercial salicylic acid cosmetics are formulated and regulated by concentration; in the EU, limits include up to 2.0 percent in most products [1]. Whether crushed aspirin delivers comparable salicylate to the skin has not been studied.

Oral aspirin is associated with stomach upset, ulcers, bleeding and worsening asthma, and is not recommended in late pregnancy or for children with viral infections because of Reye syndrome. These effects relate to oral use. For salicylic acid, Wikipedia states toxicity is mainly a concern with oral overdose, that cosmetic use poses no significant risk, and that skin and eye irritation are listed hazards; one documented case of toxicity involved a 40 percent ointment over a large body area [1]. Sources do not describe aspirin masks specifically.
No studies found. Research on salicylic acid for acne exists but does not test aspirin masks [1].

timeline.event: Johann Buchner isolates salicin from willow, the precursor line to salicylic acid. [1]
